title: Drosophila of phonon-mediated superconductivity: Full Eliashberg theory of the jellium model
authors: Christophe Berthod, Louk Rademaker, Dirk van der Marel
abstract: We present a full numerical solution of the Migdal--Eliashberg equations for the jellium model of phonon-mediated superconductivity. We find very low critical temperatures below 1~K, in contrast to earlier claims that the jellium model for hydrogen solids might reach room-temperature superconductivity. Our results suggest that full momentum and frequency dependence of the gap function and normal self-energy should be taken into account for accurate $T_c$ estimates.
summary: This work provides a rigorous, numerically intensive solution to the Migdal-Eliashberg equations for phonon-mediated superconductivity within the jellium model. The authors demonstrate that accounting for full momentum and frequency dependence drastically lowers predicted critical temperatures ($T_c < 1$ K). This result cautions against overestimating high-$T_c$ superconductivity using simplified models.
main_problem: The primary goal is to accurately determine the critical temperature ($T_c$) for phonon-mediated superconductivity in the jellium model, specifically challenging previous overestimations of high-$T_c$. The authors investigate whether the simple jellium model can support room-temperature superconductivity.
main_result: The full Eliashberg theory calculation yields very low critical temperatures ($T_c < 1$ K) for the jellium model, contradicting earlier optimistic claims. This suggests that more complex physics beyond the basic jellium framework is required for high-$T_c$.
method: The study employs a full numerical solution of the Migdal-Eliashberg equations in their momentum and frequency-dependent form, requiring advanced techniques to handle singularities near the Fermi surface.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the jellium background for phonon-mediated superconductivity. The theory relies on solving the self-consistent Eliashberg equations using approximations like Random Phase Approximation (RPA) for screening.
key_observables: Critical temperature ($T_c$), anomalous self-energy ($\Sigma_{12}$), quasiparticle residue ($Z$), and the gap function ($\Delta$).
important_parameters: Electron density ($n_e$), Chemical Potential ($\mu$), Fermi wavevector ($k_F$), and phonon frequencies ($\omega_{	ext{ph}}$).
main_assumptions: The jellium model is used, which employs the Thomas-Fermi approximation for screening and neglects effects like Friedel oscillations. The full ME equations are solved numerically, requiring approximations for momentum and frequency integration.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate characteristic energy scales ($\epsilon_F$, $\omega_s$, $k_F$) vs density; they also show the real part of the normal self-energy ($\Sigma_{11}$) and the temperature dependence of the anomalous self-energy, confirming renormalization effects.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical framework (ME equations), then tackling numerical challenges related to momentum/frequency integration, and finally presenting convergence studies leading to a low $T_c$ estimate for the jellium model.
why_interesting: While focused on BCS-like pairing in a simple metal, the rigorous application of full Eliashberg theory and the discussion of necessary approximations (RPA, momentum/frequency dependence) are highly relevant methodologies for analyzing strongly coupled quantum systems in AMO physics or condensed matter theory.
